n: Joseph formally reports to Pharaoh that his family has arrived and is waiting in Goshen, respectfully seeking official permission for them to stay.
Joseph chose five of his brothers to meet Pharaoh, a polite and manageable delegation.
When Pharaoh asked their work, they answered honestly, as Joseph advised: we are shepherds, like our fathers.
They explain they have come to live temporarily because of the famine, and they humbly ask for Goshen.
Pharaoh turns to Joseph to give his answer.
Pharaoh grants them the best land, Goshen, and even offers capable brothers jobs managing the royal herds.
Then Joseph brought in his aged father, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. The humble patriarch, bearer of the covenant, gives a blessing to the most powerful king on earth.
Pharaoh, perhaps struck by Jacob’s great age, asks how old he is.
Jacob calls his life a “pilgrimage”—a journey as a stranger. He says his 130 years have been few and hard compared to his fathers’ lives. Many trials marked his life.

f.g: sojourning; life as a traveler without a permanent home

n: Jacob blessed Pharaoh again as he left—probably a farewell blessing.
Joseph settled his family in the best land, called here the land of Rameses—a later name for the area, after the city Israel would build there.

f.g: the Goshen region, named for a later city

n: Joseph provided food for everyone, each household according to its size.

f.g: literally “according to the little ones,” by household size

n: The famine grew so severe that both Egypt and Canaan were exhausted.
Joseph collected all the money from grain sales and brought it to Pharaoh’s treasury, honestly serving his master.
When their money ran out, the Egyptians begged Joseph for bread so they would not die.
Joseph proposed trading livestock for food.
For a year, people exchanged their horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys for bread. This is one of the earliest biblical mentions of horses.
The next year they returned with nothing left to trade but their own bodies and land.
The Egyptians themselves proposed selling their land and labor to Pharaoh in exchange for food and seed to plant.
Joseph acquired all the farmland in Egypt for the crown, as people sold their fields to survive.
He relocated people into the cities, probably near the grain stores. (Some ancient texts read “made them servants” instead.)

f.g: The Greek and Samaritan versions read “he made them slaves.”

n: The priests kept their land because Pharaoh supported them with a fixed allowance—a known feature of Egyptian temples.
Joseph gives the people seed to plant on what is now Pharaoh’s land.
They would give a fifth of the harvest to Pharaoh and keep four-fifths—like a tenant-farming arrangement, a 20 percent tax.
The people were grateful, saying Joseph had saved their lives. In their eyes the arrangement was a mercy, not oppression.

f.g: Joseph’s Egyptian name may mean something like “sustainer of life.”

n: The one-fifth rule became lasting law in Egypt, with the priests exempt. “Unto this day” shows the writer’s own later time.
Meanwhile Israel settled in Goshen, acquired property, and grew rapidly—fulfilling God’s promise to make them a great nation.
Jacob lived seventeen more years in Egypt—matching the seventeen years Joseph had lived with him before being sold—and died at 147.
Near death, Israel asked Joseph to swear an oath, placing his hand under his thigh, a solemn ancient custom, promising not to bury him in Egypt.

f.w: put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh

n: Jacob wanted to be buried with Abraham and Isaac in the family tomb in Canaan—a statement of faith that God’s promise of the land would be fulfilled.

f.g: the cave of Machpelah near Hebron

n: Joseph swore, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed. Hebrews, following the Greek text, says he worshipped leaning on his staff.

f.w: bowed himself upon the bed's head
f.g: Hebrew mittah (bed) and matteh (staff) look alike when written without vowels.
